pages.text:
Grove Club was planning a small celebration under the Old Banyan.

Paper chains hung from low branches. Someone had drawn a welcome sign with crayons. The air smelled like jasmine and fresh laddoos from the snack table.

Vanshi tied the last knot on a decoration string. Her friendship bracelet caught the sunlight.

pages.text:
Aarav sat on a root with his notebook open. "Three games, one snack table, and a photo for the club wall," he read. "That should work."

Vanshi smiled. "It will feel special. I know it will."

She wanted everyone to walk in and feel cared for.

pages.text:
Then the wind came — not angry, just busy.

Paper chains lifted like birds. One fluttered into a branch and stuck.

"Oh no," Vanshi said. She ran to catch them. Her heart beat faster with every strip of paper in the air.

pages.text:
Aarav pointed at his list. "We still have time."

Vanshi nodded hard. She would fix the chains, fix the table, fix the mood — all before anyone arrived.

She wanted the day to feel special for **everyone**.

pages.text:
On the stone path, someone bumped the rangoli bowl. Pink and yellow powder spilled in a messy cloud.

Vanshi's stomach dropped. That pattern took an hour.

"It's okay," Aarav started.

But it did not feel okay. It felt like one more thing on a pile that was already too high.

pages.text:
At the snack table, the big serving bowl was gone.

"Who moved it?" Vanshi asked, louder than she meant to.

Aarav looked around. "Maybe we can find it. Or use the blue one."

Vanshi heard the worry in her own voice. Wind, spilled rangoli, missing bowl — **all at once**.

pages.text:
Vanshi grabbed the chains, the cloth, the spare rangoli cup — everything at the same time.

Aarav said, "Which one first?"

"All of them!" Vanshi snapped. "Can't you see it's all falling apart?"

She did not mean to sound sharp. But the words came out hot and fast.

pages.text:
A younger helper who had come early stopped mid-step. She had been bringing napkins.

Now she stood very still, looking at the ground.

Vanshi's chest tightened. That was not the welcome she wanted anyone to feel.

pages.text:
More helpers arrived. "Where do the cups go?" "Is the rangoli ruined?" "When do we start?"

Questions bounced like balls. Vanshi's head buzzed. Her hands wanted to do ten jobs. Her body wanted to sit down.

Everything felt **too full**.

pages.text:
Aarav did not argue. He did not say she was wrong.

He opened his notebook and wrote two words big enough to read: **Snack table. Chains.**

"Pick one," he said quietly. "We do that first. Just that."

pages.text:
Vanshi sat on the root. Her legs felt heavy. Her eyes felt wet.

"I thought if I tried hard enough, it would all stop feeling scary," she whispered.

Aarav nodded. "Sometimes everything hits at once. That is a real feeling. It is not failing."

pages.text:
Vanshi took a breath. Out loud she said, "This is too much for me right now."

The words felt strange and honest.

"Snack table first," she said. "Will you help me?"

"Yes," Aarav said. Just that.

pages.text:
They fixed the snack table together. One bowl. One row of cups. One thing **done**.

The chains could wait. The rangoli could wait.

The younger helper peeked over. Vanshi smiled — soft this time. "You can put napkins here. Thank you for coming early."

pages.text:
When the wind tugged the chains again, Vanshi did not grab them alone.

She tapped Aarav's shoulder. "Too much again. Help?"

He closed his notebook. "Let's pick one."

The celebration was not perfect. But it was beginning — and Vanshi was not carrying every piece by herself.
